longForm.overview:

The diagonal fill cue borrows from design-coded bullet lists and the modern direction-marker aesthetic, which is exactly why the emoji reads as diagonal coded rather than literal down-right-arrow-coded shape.

In real-world usage ↘️ lives in the spaces where the sender wants to communicate direction-marker energy. A partner sends it on a 'diagonal ↘️' direction-marker marker. A friend sends it on a 'down-right-pulse pulse ↘️' reveal. A coworker sends it on a 'diagonal coded ↘️' list thread. The diagonal fill cue is what makes the emoji feel diagonal coded — it is not just 'shape,' it is 'diagonal coded down-right-arrow moment.'

What separates ↘️ from the rest of the shape family is the diagonal register. The emoji is not saying 'solid-black' (⬛), 'solid-white' (⬜), or 'solid-square' (◼). It is saying 'diagonal coded down-right-arrow,' which carries a specific design-coded tradition. That is why ↘️ travels especially well on partner direction-marker markers, direction-marker reveals, and any context where the sender wants the message to land with diagonal energy.
